extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of ancient history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the author’s criteria and characterizations for what constitutes ‘civilization’ and related social forms (nomadism, bards, joint families, early states) in the Neolithic–Bronze Age narrative. Focus is on definitional conditions, distinguishing features, and historical processes described in the chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: “Civilization is something more than the occasional seasonal growing of wheat. It is the settlement of men upon an area continuously cultivated and possessed, who live in buildings continuously inhabited with a common rule and a common city or citadel.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts mere cultivation with civilization: continuity of possession and cultivation, permanent habitation in buildings, and a shared political/urban centre (city/citadel) are necessary. Examples cited: communities in Egypt and between the Euphrates and Tigris by 4000 B.C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions necessary for real settling down
rubrics_metrics.description: “The first condition necessary to a real settling down ... was of course a trustworthy all-the-year-round supply of water, fodder for the animals, food for themselves, and building material for their homes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These material prerequisites (year-round water, fodder, food, building materials) are presented as preconditions that allow sedentary life to become permanent rather than seasonal, enabling population growth, denser settlement, and the emergence of towns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics/effects of settled peoples
rubrics_metrics.description: Settled populations show multiplication and greater density, more substantial houses, extermination of wild beasts over large areas, increased security (ordinary men go about without weapons), specialization of occupations, and development of institutions like temples, writing, and hydraulic engineering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative links settlement to social and technological developments: reliable harvests and building materials produce durable dwellings and cities; specialisation (potters, carvers, priests, rulers) and public works (irrigation, brick architecture) follow. Mesopotamia (Sumerians) and Egypt are given as exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and features of nomadism
rubrics_metrics.description: Nomadism is described as a more wandering life between summer and winter pastures (migratory), with herding blended with hunting, greater reliance on milk, breeding cattle for milk, leaner diets, and a more active, warlike existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nomads are portrayed as mobile, often more warlike, and quicker adopters of new weapons/transport (horses, chariots, possibly early iron). Their economy and social organization differ from settled agriculturists, and they frequently raid settled borders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction cycle between nomads and settled peoples (conquest→settlement→refinement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurring historical pattern: border raiding by nomads; occasional unification of nomadic tribes under leaders who conquer settled regions; conquerors settle, appropriate land and labour, become rulers/aristocrats, intermarry and adopt the conquered civilization’s refinements, then later are themselves vulnerable to fresh invasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author presents this alternation of settlement, conquest, refinement, and fresh conquest as one of the main long-term processes of history over millennia, accounting for formation of ruling classes, changes in social structure, and cycles of cultural assimilation and military renewal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and qualities of bards / oral tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Bards (rhapsodists) chanted or recited stories of the past and present; they developed rhythms, rhymes, alliteration, and likely helped elaborate and fix grammatical forms. They were 'the first great artists of the ear' and acted as living books preserving traditions (sagas, epics, vedas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bards are credited with sustaining collective memory and identity before widespread writing; even after the introduction of writing they persisted (e.g., minstrels). Their oral revisions mean surviving epics are often altered from prehistoric originals; examples include the Iliad and the Odyssey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epics/sagas/vedas as historical sources
rubrics_metrics.description: “These sagas, epics, and vedas do supply, in addition to archæology and philology, a third source of information about those vanished times.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats oral epics as a complementary source of historical evidence, usable alongside archaeology and philology. He illustrates with poetic passages (Iliad describing burial/barrow construction) and later sagas like Beowulf that preserve ritual details (pyres, mounds, funerary treasures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political and religious structure of early Aryan/Greek societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Aryan/Greek societies had chiefs who were heads of families and performed sacrifices; priests were primarily keepers of shrines; when going to war elders appointed a king with loosely defined powers; there were no laws but customs and no exact standards of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion describes a weak centralized authority in peacetime, ritualized leader roles, and customary (not legal) norms. Military leadership could be situational (king appointed for war); religious life lacked deep sacramental structures—priests functioned as shrine-keepers rather than a distinct learned class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint family (household) structure and obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The joint family is described as 'a co-operative corporation' with a senior member at the head, all able-bodied contributing labour/earnings to common stock, weaker members maintained, strong family ties, a family deity and household priest, servants treated as part of the family, and customary duties of hospitality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Basu’s quoted account is used to exemplify a household organization that persisted from Neolithic types into modern Hindu communities: multi-generational co-residence, collective economic responsibility, caste-related service roles, informal education (resident teacher), and ritual obligations that bind the group together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material/craft and urban indicators of early civilization (Sumerian example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sumerian civilization is characterized by use of clay/brick architecture, irrigation/hydraulic engineering, pottery/earthenware, cuneiform writing scratched on clay, temple tower-buildings, and city-state political organization with military capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These material-cultural markers (brick towers, irrigation, writing on clay, temple institutions, standing armies) are presented as concrete indicators of urban civilization in the Euphrates–Tigris valley; their longevity and technical achievements (e.g., cuneiform, shipping) are emphasized.
